citation.title: A systematic review of moral agency in artificial agents
citation.venue: Discover Psychology6:9; first online2025, version of record2026

reading.source_scope_note: Narrative systematic review of36 publications about perceived moral agency and proximal judgments such as blame, moral standing, rights and trust. These are human attributions to artificial agents, not evidence that robots actually have moral agency, consciousness or rights. No meta-analysis or new participant study.
access_limits: All supplied text, table, native flowchart and full public36-row supplement read. All36 original publications were not independently fully read for this review; their samples/effects remain secondary reports.

Earlier project reviews23/24/79 fully read overlapping manuscripts/publications; this review does not turn their reuse into new participant samples. Review23 is an early manuscript, so exact equivalence with the final CSCW version is not assumed.

Search date/window endpoints, database-specific search logs, independent screening counts, source-level risk-of-bias appraisal and an effect-size synthesis are not supplied. No search or complete selection reproduction claimed.
Selected Crossref/publisher metadata checks establish identity and citation fields, not independent full-reading credit for books, clinical trials or scale validations.
No author contact, participant dataset request, clinical recommendation or actual AI moral-status determination. Same-context checking is not an independent audit.

study.design: PsycINFO, Scopus, IEEE and ACM search; stated Boolean3rd-party agent terms AND morality/agency terms, while narrative also describes an initial OR-only harvest. English articles over a loosely described last two decades and citation harvesting. Only experiments/surveys in synthesis; ethnography used for contextual implications.
study.unit: Thirty-six publication rows are present in both main overview and Detailed Table1. Multi-experiment publications are not36 single experiments, and the review adds no new participants.
study.flow: Native Figure1:11822−6701=5121;5121−4985=136. Listed full-text exclusions19+83+2+1+2+1=108, leaving28, whereas database inclusion says27. Citation search14−6=8. Printed27+8=35, not total36. The inferred28+8 would equal36 but is not a verified replacement; exact screening records needed.
study.category_counts: Agent-type section says25 papers but its explicit list[2,28–32,34–49] has22 unique reference IDs. Behavior section has9 unique studies and separates8 positive/mixed from1 weak/null. Modality section says4 studies but cites only31,32,53 and counts53 again as mixed; remaining33 would fit3 unique studies. Do not equate vote counts with independent effect sizes or proof of a moderator.
study.measurement: Direct Perceived Moral Agency scales are sparse. Blame, punishment, rights, fairness, agency/experience, Godspeed/RoSAS/NARS and perceived trust are heterogeneous outcomes rather than interchangeable validated PMA measures.
study.conceptual_boundary: The definition emphasizes attributed moral/agentic capacities. Moral wrongness of an act, blame of an actor, concern for a target’s welfare, social standing and legally justified duties are distinct. An agent can be judged blameworthy while not thought capable of suffering; absence of rights is not by itself proof of absent agency.
study.heterogeneity: Appearance, embodiment, modality, social behavior, control information and stakes vary together across publications. Some source designs compare countries/samples or live/video across separate experiments. Narrative comparisons do not isolate culture, developmental change, embodiment or temporal trends.
study.self_blame: Preference for self-blaming robots and lower willingness to collaborate with user-blaming robots are reported from separate small studies. User comfort does not determine factual responsibility. Distinguish likability, trust and warranted attribution; no advice to give false confessions.
study.demographics: Gender often not reported or tested; this does not establish absence of an effect. Age comparisons include different agent modalities and studies, not a single longitudinal developmental trajectory. US versus heterogeneous non-US samples is not a uniform cultural contrast.
study.clinical_implications: PARO pain/mood/oxytocin and dementia-care claims are external contextual literature, not36 direct-PMA outcomes or evidence that moral-agency attribution is a necessary therapeutic mechanism. Biomarker changes do not independently identify empathy, stress reduction or clinical efficacy.
study.supplement_checks: Komatsu row printsN1285 but country counts518+811=1329; cannot choose correctedN from these fields alone. Monroe Study1 lists five groups33+37+43+43+41=197 while calling them four. Stuart/Kneer row describes3×2 but reports a harm/no-harm outcome too; earlier preprint review23 explicitly has3×2×2. Original final model not re-read here.

summary: Enrich existing moral-agency attribution, human–robot moral judgment asymmetry, moral standing, scapegoating, social presence and reciprocity. Partial/emergent PMA and moral disqualification remain context-dependent refinements rather than new synonym rows. Record flow/sample/category inconsistencies, sparse direct measures and publication reuse. Do not turn favorable anthropomorphic responses into actual mentality, justified responsibility or clinical benefit.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity the capacity to understand moral considerations, make ethical judgments and bear responsibility for its choices.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.

evidence.quote: perception that artificial agents have moral

findings.evidence_scope: The36-publication review synthesizes direct PMA ratings and indirect judgments. It describes partial, graded, relational and context-dependent attribution; direct moral-capacity measures are uncommon. This supports a human perception construct, not a finding that current AI actually understands ethics.
findings.boundary: Moral/agentic attribution, blame, patienthood, legal rights and actual capacity differ. Sparse proxy evidence, narrative vote counting and no longitudinal test do not establish one unified mechanism or a historical rise in actual agency.

findings.definition: Differences in moral evaluations of otherwise matched decisions attributed to human versus artificial agents.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.

evidence.quote: robots are blamed more for inaction than action

findings.evidence_scope: The review describes action/inaction blame patterns varying with human, mechanical robot, humanoid or drone framing and command-role information. It retains counterexamples and culture/context variation; this is a conditional evaluation pattern.
findings.boundary: Different expectations may reflect relevant assigned duties rather than irrational bias. Null contrasts are not equivalence, and comparisons across source studies are not a formal agent×culture×modality interaction. Do not assume all robots are always blamed more.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.
findings.evidence_scope: Children’s responses to social robots and adult rights surveys are synthesized as attributions of consideration, sometimes stronger after emotional protest. Welfare, moral standing and sociopolitical rights are different endpoints.
findings.boundary: Protest or emotional display can elicit concern without proving actual suffering, moral agency or rights. Preserve human dignity independently of these tasks. The review’s age trend is not a universal developmental rule or permission to manipulate children’s attachments.

findings.definition: Deflecting personal or collective responsibility for a negative outcome by directing blame toward another person, group or entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.

evidence.quote: used as scapegoats for human moral faults

findings.evidence_scope: The review discusses moral shielding when primary AI decision-making lowers attributed fault toward human monitors compared with solo humans. It also acknowledges indirect evidence and continued substantial human blame.
findings.boundary: A rating difference does not establish deliberate evasion, actual release from legal liability or unjust attribution in every case. AI as a blame absorber differs from a human operator becoming a Moral crumple zone; trace actual roles and evidence.

findings.definition: The subjective sense that another social actor is real and present during an interaction.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.
findings.evidence_scope: A small set of live, image/video and text studies motivates presence/embodiment as possible contributors to social and moral responses. Some effects are mixed or fail to carry from online to live settings.
findings.boundary: Physical embodiment, visual information and subjective social presence differ. Cross-experiment samples, assignment and interaction opportunities can vary; stronger PMA from embodiment is not a universally isolated causal effect. Subjective presence does not prove consciousness.

findings.definition: Receiving a benefit creates an expectation or pressure to return a benefit.
findings.novelty_rationale: A narrative synthesis of an existing attribution or social-response construct, not a distinct new behavior or independent replication of every cited study.

evidence.quote: Reciprocal conduct also elicits moral responses

findings.evidence_scope: The review reports that prior helpfulness by a robot can increase later assistance/compliance. This is secondary support for direct reciprocity, not a new experiment or a demonstration of felt mutual care.
findings.boundary: Repaying a favor differs from emotion reciprocity and indirect reputation-based cooperation. Helpful responses must not manufacture obligations, demand personal disclosure or encourage unsafe compliance. Prior assistance does not establish AI feelings.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Full-text exclusions total108, so136 leaves28 rather than27. Other-method14−6=8, and27+8=35 rather than36. Main and supplementary tables each list36 rows. Exact reconciliation requires screening records; do not silently replace inclusion count or manufacture an extra report.
Printed total1285 differs from518US+811Japan=1329. Recruitment versus retained counts could differ, but no reconciliation was verified. No corrected sample size invented.

The25 agent-type count is paired with22 unique citation IDs. Modality says4 studies but references3 unique publications, reusing Lee53 for a mixed outcome, while33remaining fits3. Need source-level category coding before corrected counts.

Often unreported gender effects do not establish gender irrelevance. Different samples/modalities cannot identify a pure age or culture mechanism. A cross-sectional historical corpus does not demonstrate increasing PMA over time or a direct link from empathy to actual moral agency.

Pain, mood, dementia-care and salivary oxytocin findings are outside direct PMA evidence. Their causal connection to attributed moral agency or empathy is not tested by this review. Primary PARO papers were not fully read here; biomarker meaning is not reduced to a universal stress rule.

The Stuart/Kneer row omits the outcome factor from its stated design while describing its result. Earlier full preprint review23 includes that factor; final version not independently re-read here. Other country, sample and modality assertions remain secondary, not verified original datasets.

methodological_limits: Thirty-six heterogeneous publications, not36 direct-PMA experiments or independent replications. A small number of direct measures is mixed with blame, trust, rights, agency and patiency proxies.

No explicit search end date or database-specific reproducible history, no reported meta-analysis or source-level risk-of-bias appraisal. The initial OR-only strategy differs from the displayed AND query and needs exact logs.
PRISMA and sample/category arithmetic discrepancies are recorded without guessed repairs. Their presence does not establish fabricated sources, intent or misconduct.

Non-significant contrasts are not equivalence, cross-study differences are not formal moderation and behavioral preference is not evidence of actual AI mentality. Theoretical agency prerequisites are not empirically proved by these ratings.
Partial/emergent moral agency and moral disqualification describe existing attribution patterns; do not inflate the ontology with labels for positive/negative directions of the same appraisal.

Greater liking for self-blaming robots does not justify inaccurate self-blame, flattery or concealment of human accountability. Keep factual explanation and warranted responsibility separate from user comfort.
Contextual clinical and book references receive no independent full-reading credit. No public long-term efficacy or demographic rule is established by this review.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The early Guilty Artificial Minds manuscript independently read here includes3×2×2 design and513 retained participants. The review’s shortened design description should not overwrite that detailed version-specific evidence.

Playing the Blame Game’s owner-blame capacity effect only trends atp.055; sophistication descriptions bundle capacities. Avoid converting its secondary blame-shifting account into a proven necessary theory-of-mind mechanism.

Banks2020online/2021issue is already fully reviewed. Its live/video comparisons also vary sampling/assignment; the significant fairness interaction concerns goodness, not an automatically significant responsibility interaction. Preserve those distinctions.

AI acting as a moral shield and a clinician becoming a liability sink can run in different directions. Both require role-sensitive responsibility analysis, not an assumption that blame always disappears or always concentrates on humans.

deferred.term: Partial/emergent moral agency and moral disqualification
deferred.reason: Contextual degree/direction refinements of Moral agency attribution, not independently defined mechanisms warranting duplicate rows.
The described responsibility deflection overlaps Moral scapegoating. Retain the named context and need for actual allocation evidence.

deferred.term: Bodily coordinated motion as a distinct moral mechanism
deferred.reason: One small secondary study describes a joint handle task but does not isolate coordination as the causal moral mechanism. Read a defining primary source and compare motor coordination/synchrony before adding a new construct.

limitations: Zero new entries; existing categories/IDs preserved. No independent credit for unread originals, automatic harm/principle edges, forced citation quota, invented timeline counts or full-paper Markdown transcription.
